# Marrow-Class Ferry Handbook

## Dawn departure checks

The deck crew starts the Marrow-class ferry's ballast pumps 25 minutes before the first sailing and lets them run until the trim gauge settles, because a ferry that leaves the slip with water still shifting in the forward tank rolls at the harbour mouth and frightens the commuters. The pumps are checked by sound as much as by gauge, and a pump that hunts or whines is reported to the engineer before the lines are cast off, not after the crossing.

The mooring lines are inspected for chafe at the fairleads every morning. A line with more than three broken strands in one lay is condemned on the spot, and the spare lines live in the blue locker under the forward bench. The deck crew writes the condemned line's length in the log so the chandler can be told how much to send, and the old line is cut into fenders rather than thrown away.

Passenger counts are tallied at the gangway by the clicker, and the ferry is full at 148 passengers on the upper deck and lower deck together. When the count reaches the limit the deckhand raises the red flag and the ticket office is told by radio, so that nobody is sold a ticket for a sailing that cannot carry them and nobody is left arguing on the slip.

In fog the horn sounds one long blast every two minutes while under way, and the radar is kept on the short range so the mooring buoys show clearly. The master slows to four knots inside the breakwater regardless of the timetable, and a late sailing is always preferred to a close call with the oyster barges that work the channel before dawn.

The fuel tanks are dipped on Friday afternoons and topped up when they fall below a third. The engineer signs the dip sheet, and the master countersigns it, so that a shortage can never be put down to one person's arithmetic. The last Friday of the month the sheets go to the harbour office, where they are filed beside the oil records for the year.
